subtype: Writing what is in the head [Actor]
passage: Kaito, nine, wrote about his weekend for the class newsletter: "We went there and did it, and then we ate it. It was so good." In his head there was the lake, the paddle boat with a broken seat, and the rice balls his grandfather had packed. Felix, who sat next to him, read the page and frowned. "Went where? Did what? Ate what?" Kaito was puzzled. It was all so clear to him. He picked up his pencil and asked himself what Felix would need if Felix had not been there. He added the name of the lake, the paddle boat, and the rice balls his grandfather had packed. Felix read it again and grinned. "Now I can see it."

qa.q: What did Kaito write first about his weekend?
qa.a: Kaito wrote that they went there and did it, and then ate it, and it was so good.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling when Felix asked "Went where?"
qa.a: Puzzled, because it all seemed clear in his head.

qa.q: What did Kaito add that helped Felix understand?
qa.a: Kaito added the name of the lake, the paddle boat and the rice balls his grandfather had packed.

qa.q: How did Felix see the first page?
qa.a: Felix found it confusing, since it did not say where, what or which food, and could picture it only after the details were added.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild who writes as if the reader already knows the story, leaving out obvious steps, then adds them from the reader's viewpoint.

subtype: Writing what is in the head [Actor]
passage: In Class 5, Keerthana finished the science answer first: "The seed grows because of the water and then it becomes big." She had watered the bean in the class window for two weeks, and the roots, the leaves and the first flower were all in her memory. Imran Sir, marking notebooks, put a small question mark and wrote: "Which seed? What did you see first? What happened next?" Keerthana read it twice. "But I know it," she whispered. "Yes," the teacher smiled, "but I wasn't there. I only have your page." She pulled her notebook back and wrote the steps in order: soaked, planted, roots on day four, leaves on day nine. This time there was no question mark.

qa.q: How long had Keerthana been watering the bean?
qa.a: Keerthana had watered the bean in the class window for two weeks.

qa.q: What did Keerthana feel when she whispered "But I know it"?
qa.a: Puzzled and a little defensive, since the answer felt complete to her.

qa.q: What step did Keerthana take after the teacher's questions?
qa.a: She wrote the events in order: soaked, planted, roots on day four, leaves on day nine.

qa.q: Why might Imran Sir have asked questions instead of simply correcting the answer?
qa.a: So that Keerthana could discover for herself what a reader who was not there needs to know, in a kind way. 🙂

grounding: Shows a schoolchild leaving out steps that seem obvious to her when writing an answer, and learning to take the reader's viewpoint.

subtype: Writing what is in the head [Actor]
passage:
In Class Four, we read a story about a boy and a kite. The question was, "Why did Raju cry?" I wrote: "Because it broke."
I was sure it was right. I had read the story. I knew what broke.
Miss wrote in red: "What broke? Why did it matter?" I felt cross. It was obvious!
At home I showed it to my big brother Samir. He read my answer and said, "Hafsa, what broke? The kite? His leg? His heart?" He laughed, and I laughed too, a little.
Then I wrote it again: "Raju cried because his new kite got stuck in the tree and the string broke, and his papa had made it for him."
It was longer, but now someone who had not read the story would know.

qa.q: What did Hafsa first write as the answer?
qa.a: Hafsa wrote: "Because it broke."

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when Miss wrote in red?
qa.a: Hafsa felt cross, because the answer seemed obvious after reading the story.

qa.q: What could Hafsa try next time to check an answer?
qa.a: Hafsa could read the answer as if they had never read the story, or ask someone at home to read it.

qa.q: How does Samir see Hafsa's first answer?
qa.a: Samir finds it funny and unclear, and he uses a joke to show there were many things that could have broken.

grounding: Illustrates a child who writes as if the reader already knows the story and learns to add the missing steps.

subtype: Writing what is in the head [Actor]
passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5B, Friday.
Parul wrote an excited account of our trip to the planetarium, but I could not follow it. It said: "Then we waited and waited and then it was fixed and we went in." Fixed what? Went in where?
I asked Parul to read it aloud to her partner, Uday, who had been absent that day. Uday listened and asked, "What was fixed?" Parul blinked. "The bus! The tyre went flat!" She stared at her page. "But I know that," she said.
"You do," I said. "Uday doesn't."
She took the notebook back and added two sentences about the flat tyre and the man who came to change it. She read it to Uday again. He nodded.
I will try partner-reading with the whole class next week; a real reader helps children see the gaps.
— Class teacher, 5B

qa.q: Where did the class go on the trip?
qa.a: They went to the planetarium.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when she said, "But I know that"?
qa.a: Parul was surprised and a little puzzled, realising the flat tyre was clear in her own head but not on the page.

qa.q: Why did reading aloud to Uday help Parul?
qa.a: Uday had missed the trip, so his question showed exactly which step Parul had left out.

qa.q: How might Uday feel after Parul reads the new version?
qa.a: Uday likely feels pleased and included, since now he can follow what happened on the trip.

grounding: Shows a child who leaves out steps that seem obvious to her and discovers the gap when a real reader cannot follow.

subtype: Writing what is in the head [Actor]
passage:
Dear Diary,
Today I wrote how to make a paper boat for my cousin Usha. She is little.
I wrote: 1. Fold it. 2. Fold the corners. 3. Open it and make a boat.
Usha tried at my table. She held the paper and said, "Sudha didi, fold it which way?" Then she folded a corner the wrong way and the paper tore. Her lip wobbled.
I felt bad. And annoyed, because I KNOW how to make it!
So I did it very slowly, and I wrote every single step while I did it. Fold in half the long way. Fold again to make a crease. It became nine steps!
Usha made her boat with my new list. It floated in the bucket 🙂 Next time I write steps, I will do it slowly first.
Sudha

qa.q: How many steps did the new list have?
qa.a: It became nine steps.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when Usha's paper tore?
qa.a: Sudha felt bad for Usha and also annoyed, because Sudha knew how to make the boat without thinking.

qa.q: What worked better the second time, and why?
qa.a: Doing it very slowly and writing every step while doing it, because it caught the steps Sudha had skipped.

qa.q: What was it like for Usha when the first list didn't work?
qa.a: Usha felt confused and upset; she asked which way to fold, and her lip wobbled when the paper tore.

grounding: Illustrates a child who writes instructions that skip obvious-to-her steps and learns to write them from the reader's view.

subtype: Writing what is in the head [Actor]
passage: On Friday, Devika wrote directions on a notebook page so that Trisha could come to her house in the village for the Pongal kolam on Sunday. "From school, go past the tree and turn at the shop. My house is the blue one." She folded it proudly. On Sunday Devika waited at the gate with a plate of sugarcane. Trisha didn't come. At last a bicycle bell rang, and Trisha jumped off her father's bicycle, cross and hot. "Which tree? There are fifty trees! Which shop? I went to the tea shop and the ration shop, and nobody's house was blue!" Devika blinked. The tree was the big tamarind, of course. The shop was Murugan anna's shop, of course. Everybody knew that. Then she looked at Trisha's red face and thought, maybe not everybody.

qa.q: What did Devika's directions say about her house?
qa.a: "My house is the blue one."

qa.q: How did Devika feel when Trisha asked which tree and which shop?
qa.a: Devika was surprised and puzzled, because the tamarind and Murugan anna's shop seemed obvious, and then began to realise they weren't obvious to Trisha.

qa.q: What could Devika add to her directions next time?
qa.a: Name the exact landmarks, like "the big tamarind tree" and "Murugan anna's shop", and imagine walking the route as someone who has never been there.

qa.q: What was the search like for Trisha?
qa.a: Trisha felt lost and frustrated, trying the tea shop and the ration shop and arriving hot and cross after all the wrong turns.

grounding: Shows a child who writes directions assuming the reader already knows the landmarks and leaves out what seems obvious to her.
